screens.title: Iterator and Template Method Patterns
screens.subtitle: Traverse collections cleanly. Define algorithm skeletons safely.

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn two complementary behavioral patterns that help make code clearer and more maintainable. First, the Iterator pattern gives you a single, consistent way to traverse elements in any collection without exposing the collection's internal structure. You will see why that decoupling matters with a custom BookShelf example and how a simple iterator interface prevents client code from depending on arrays or linked nodes. Second, the Template Method pattern lets you fix the high-level algorithm while letting subclasses implement details. You will follow a BeverageMaker example and a ReportGenerator scenario to practice creating template methods, hooks, and concrete overrides. Along the way we'll highlight common mistakes: modifying a collection while iterating and making a template method non-final. By the end of the chapter you'll be able to choose which pattern fits a problem, implement a custom iterator in Java, and structure algorithms so new variants can be added without changing existing code. A brief practical activity is included so you can apply the Template Method to a report generator and reinforce what you learned.

keyIdea.title: Why these patterns matter
keyIdea.text: Iterator decouples traversal from storage. Template Method enforces an algorithm's structure while allowing safe customization. Together they increase reuse and reduce coupling.

narration.text: By the end of these lessons you will be able to explain why the Iterator pattern separates traversal from representation, and why that separation reduces coupling in client code. You will implement a custom iterator for a simple collection in Java, including correct hasNext and next behavior and safe error handling when the iteration ends. You will also understand the Template Method pattern: how to define a final template method, which abstract methods subclasses must implement, and when to use hook methods. Finally you'll learn to apply both patterns where they improve flexibility and maintainability — for example, using Iterator to traverse a custom BookShelf and using Template Method to structure report generation or beverage preparation so subclasses supply specific steps without changing the algorithm flow. Each objective includes a small visual mnemonic to help you recall the skill and a verified competency milestone that points to hands-on work that proves mastery.

screens.title: Iterator Pattern — What and Why
screens.subtitle: Provide a standard traversal without exposing internals

narration.text: The Iterator pattern gives you a simple contract for walking a collection so clients never need to know whether data is in an array, a linked structure, or something else. Concretely, an iterator presents methods such as hasNext and next. hasNext returns a boolean indicating whether more elements remain, while next returns the next element and advances the iterator. This decoupling prevents client code from being tightly bound to a collection's internal nodes or array indices. Imagine you have a linked list and later change it to a compact array for performance. If clients relied on nodes or indexes, many places would need changing. With an iterator, only the concrete iterator changes. A concrete iterator keeps internal position state and implements the iteration logic. A common misconception is that iterators duplicate the collection’s storage; they do not. Iterators reference the collection but encapsulate traversal behavior. Another important point: iterators should handle end-of-iteration cleanly, typically by throwing a well-known exception or by ensuring hasNext guards calls to next. As a quick example, picture a BookShelf that returns a CustomIterator. The BookShelf keeps its array internally; the iterator knows the array and a position index. Clients use hasNext and next and remain oblivious to whether BookShelf uses an array or a different backing store. How does this affect your design choices? Prefer iterators when traversal logic might vary or when you want to protect internal representation.

keyIdea.title: Iterator definition
keyIdea.text: Iterator exposes hasNext and next so clients traverse without depending on a collection's structure.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Iterator Pattern
Definition

Iterator provides sequential access

It decouples traversal logic from the collection implementation so clients can iterate uniformly.

Core methods
  • hasNext(): returns true if elements remain
  • next(): returns element and advances the iterator
Misconception
Iterators do not copy storage; they reference the collection and encapsulate traversal state.
Key Takeaway

Use iterators to keep traversal centralized and make collection internals replaceable without changing clients.

Concrete Example
A BookShelf keeps an internal array of strings. It returns a BookShelfIterator that holds the array and a position index. The client asks hasNext and next to consume titles without touching array indices.
Illustrative code
interface CustomIterator<T> { boolean hasNext(); T next(); }
class BookShelfIterator implements CustomIterator<String> {
  private String[] books; private int position = 0;
  public BookShelfIterator(String[] books){ this.books = books; }
  public boolean hasNext(){ return position < books.length; }
  public String next(){ if(!hasNext()) throw new java.util.NoSuchElementException(); return books[position++]; }
}
Example takeaway: the client never needs to know about the array; only the iterator implementation does. That protects the collection's internal representation while allowing traversal.

narration.text: The pattern is often described with four participants that work together. First, the Iterator interface declares the traversal contract — typically hasNext and next. Second, ConcreteIterator implements that contract and holds traversal state, such as an index or a pointer to the current node. Third, the Aggregate interface declares a method to create an iterator, for example createIterator or iterator. Fourth, ConcreteAggregate implements the collection and returns the correct ConcreteIterator for its internal structure. Together they decouple clients from storage details: clients ask the aggregate for an iterator and then use the iterator to traverse elements. A useful mental model is to think of the aggregate as a building and the iterator as a guide who knows the floor plan. If you replace the building with a different layout, you only change the guide, not the tourists. The design also supports multiple concurrent iterators on the same aggregate, each with its own traversal state, and it makes custom traversal strategies possible — for example, skipping null entries or iterating in reverse. A common pitfall is letting clients access internal pointers or exposing the backing array directly; keep creation of iterators as the only access point for traversal.

keyIdea.title: Pattern participants
keyIdea.text: Four roles: Iterator and ConcreteIterator handle traversal; Aggregate and ConcreteAggregate provide creation and storage.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Iterator Participants
Participant Summary
  • Iterator: declares hasNext and next.
  • ConcreteIterator: implements traversal and tracks position.
  • Aggregate: declares createIterator.
  • ConcreteAggregate: returns an appropriate iterator instance.
Practical notes
Design your ConcreteIterator to hold minimal state and not expose internal collection fields. If you need different traversal orders, implement different ConcreteIterator classes rather than adding traversal logic to the collection itself.
Example Assembly
BookShelf (ConcreteAggregate)
Stores titles and returns a BookShelfIterator via createIterator.
BookShelfIterator (ConcreteIterator)
Holds internal array and index; implements hasNext and next.
Pro tip

When you need fail-fast behavior, have the iterator capture a modification count and compare it during traversal to detect concurrent modifications.

screens.title: BookShelf and Custom Aggregate
screens.subtitle: Designing a simple collection that creates an iterator

narration.text: Let's step through the BookShelf concrete aggregate so you can implement createIterator correctly. The BookShelf maintains an internal array of book titles and a counter that tracks how many books are stored. Its public A P I includes addBook, getBookAt, getLength, and createIterator. The key design decision is to keep the array private and only return an iterator for traversal. The createIterator method returns a BookShelfIterator instance, usually passing the internal array or a snapshot of it. Passing the raw array is acceptable for single-threaded examples, but in production you might return an iterator that observes modifications or uses a defensive copy, depending on performance and safety needs. A common student error is exposing the internal array directly through a getter. Avoid that: expose only the iterator so the collection can change its internal representation later without breaking clients. In code, addBook should only mutate internal fields; createIterator should instantiate the iterator with whatever internal reference is necessary. Testing the BookShelf by adding books and then consuming them with the iterator demonstrates the decoupling. If you later replace the array with linked nodes, you rewrite the iterator but clients remain unchanged. Try to design addBook to handle bounds gracefully and ensure getLength returns the number of valid elements for the iterator to use.

keyIdea.title: Aggregate design
keyIdea.text: Keep storage private and provide iterator creation as the only traversal access point to protect internals.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › BookShelf Aggregate
BookShelf API
  • constructor(int maxSize): allocate backing array
  • addBook(String): append if space available
  • getBookAt(int): internal access for iterator
  • getLength(): number of stored items
  • createIterator(): returns a CustomIterator
Design note
Prefer createIterator as the only traversal entry point. Avoid exposing the backing array via public getters.
Illustrative code
class BookShelf implements CustomAggregate<String> {
  private String[] books; private int last = 0;
  public BookShelf(int maxSize){ this.books = new String[maxSize]; }
  public void addBook(String book){ if(last < books.length) books[last++] = book; else System.err.println("BookShelf is full!"); }
  public String getBookAt(int index){ return books[index]; }
  public int getLength(){ return last; }
  public CustomIterator<String> createIterator(){ return new BookShelfIterator(this.books); }
}
If thread-safety is required, consider returning an iterator that checks a modification count or use defensive copying depending on performance trade-offs.

screens.title: BookShelfIterator — hasNext & next
screens.subtitle: Implementing traversal state and end-of-iteration behavior

narration.text: Now focus on the iterator itself. The BookShelfIterator needs to hold a reference to the backing array and an integer position that indicates the next element to return. Implement hasNext to compare position against the array length, but be mindful that the aggregate may store fewer valid entries than the array length if it supports sparse storage. In our BookShelf example, the aggregate keeps a last counter; you might prefer passing the last value into the iterator or passing a snapshot array sized to last to make hasNext simple. Implement next to first check hasNext and throw a standard NoSuchElementException if there are no remaining elements. This explicit check avoids silent errors and signals clients of incorrect usage. Also, document whether the iterator is fail-fast: a naive iterator will not detect concurrent modifications; a fail-fast variant captures a modification count from the aggregate in its constructor and compares it on each next or hasNext call, throwing ConcurrentModificationException if it changes. A common rookie mistake is advancing position in next before returning the element; that works but ensure you return the correct element and update state atomically. Test the iterator by iterating until hasNext is false and confirm that calling next afterward throws the expected exception.

keyIdea.title: Iterator implementation details
keyIdea.text: Track traversal state internally, guard next with hasNext, and decide whether to detect concurrent modifications for safety.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › BookShelfIterator
Essential behavior
  • Keep a reference to the aggregate's data or a snapshot.
  • Maintain a position index that starts at zero.
  • hasNext compares position against available elements.
  • next checks hasNext, returns element, then advances position.
Error handling
Callers should use hasNext before next. If next is called without elements remaining, throw NoSuchElementException to make misuse obvious.
Iterator code
class BookShelfIterator implements CustomIterator<String> {
  private String[] books; private int position = 0;
  public BookShelfIterator(String[] books){ this.books = books; }
  public boolean hasNext(){ return position < books.length && books[position] != null; }
  public String next(){ if(!hasNext()) throw new java.util.NoSuchElementException(); return books[position++]; }
}
Tip: if the collection tracks the number of valid entries, pass that into the iterator to avoid checking for nulls at each step.

screens.title: Using an Iterator — Client Code Pattern
screens.subtitle: Safe traversal, checking hasNext and handling end conditions

narration.text: When you consume an iterator, adopt a simple, robust pattern: first obtain the iterator from the aggregate, then while hasNext is true call next to retrieve elements. This pattern is succinct and hides traversal complexity. A typical mistake is intermixing direct collection access and iterator usage; pick one approach and keep it consistent so code remains maintainable. Another issue arises when a collection is modified during iteration. If you add or remove elements while another piece of code is iterating, you risk missing elements or seeing inconsistent state. Java's fail-fast iterators mitigate this by recording a modification count at creation and comparing it during iteration, throwing ConcurrentModificationException if a mismatch is detected. If you need to support concurrent modifications safely, either synchronize access or use concurrent collections that provide weakly consistent iterators. For single-threaded examples like our BookShelf demo, demonstrate client code by creating the BookShelf, adding a few titles, obtaining the iterator, and printing each title until no elements remain. Finally, always test edge cases: empty collections and calling next without checking hasNext should be intentionally covered to ensure your code handles them predictably.

keyIdea.title: Client traversal pattern
keyIdea.text: Obtain iterator, loop with hasNext, call next; avoid modifying the collection while iterating unless using concurrent-safe structures.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Using an Iterator
Client pattern
BookShelf shelf = new BookShelf(4);
shelf.addBook("The Lord of the Rings");
shelf.addBook("1984");
CustomIterator<String> it = shelf.createIterator();
while(it.hasNext()){
  String book = it.next();
  System.out.println("Book: " + book);
}
This pattern keeps client code readable and independent of the collection's layout.
Concurrent modification
If you mutate the collection after creating the iterator, results may be inconsistent. Java's fail-fast iterators detect structural changes by comparing a modification counter and throw an exception. For thread-safe iteration, use specialized concurrent collections or synchronize access.
Common mistake

Modifying the collection while iterating can cause skipped elements or runtime exceptions. Ensure you design for safe mutation or disallow it while iterating.

screens.title: Template Method Pattern — Definition and Motivation
screens.subtitle: Fix the algorithm flow, vary the steps

narration.text: The Template Method pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in an abstract base class while delegating specific steps to subclasses. The base class implements the high-level procedure as a template method, often marked final to prevent subclasses from changing the sequence. The template calls abstract methods and optional hooks; subclasses implement those to provide behavior for particular steps. This pattern is useful when you have a fixed process that varies in details. For example, preparing a beverage involves boiling water, brewing, pouring, and adding condiments. The order is invariant, but brewing and condiments differ between coffee and tea. Template Method enforces consistency — clients call the template method and know the process order will be followed. A misconception is that template classes should be empty shells; instead the abstract class should provide common concrete steps to reduce duplication. Another pitfall is offering too many abstract methods, which makes the abstract class lose its role as a meaningful template. Use hooks sparingly to provide optional behavior without forcing subclasses to implement them. When designed well, Template Method adheres to the Open/Closed Principle: you can add new concrete subclasses without changing the template or existing code.

keyIdea.title: Template Method
keyIdea.text: Template Method fixes an algorithm's order and calls abstract or hook methods for subclass-specific behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Template Method
Pattern idea

Algorithm skeleton with customizable steps

Define prepareBeverage as final so the order is enforced. Subclasses implement brew and addCondiments to vary results.

Hook methods
Hooks provide optional customization. They can have default implementations so subclasses may override them if needed.
Example summary
BeverageMaker.prepareBeverage calls boilWater, brew, pourInCup, addCondiments in that order. CoffeeMaker implements brew and addCondiments differently than TeaMaker, but both follow the same sequence.
Key takeaway

Use Template Method to enforce consistent algorithm order while allowing subclasses to supply the variable pieces.

screens.title: BeverageMaker Example — Template Method in Java
screens.subtitle: prepareBeverage final method and subclass overrides

narration.text: Walk through the BeverageMaker template example to see Template Method in action. The abstract base class defines a final prepareBeverage method that calls common concrete steps and abstract steps. Concrete methods like boilWater and pourInCup are implemented in the base class because they don't vary between beverages. The abstract methods brew and addCondiments are left for subclasses. When CoffeeMaker implements brew it performs a drip through a filter; addCondiments adds sugar and milk. TeaMaker implements brew by steeping and addCondiments by adding lemon. This organization keeps the algorithm order fixed and moves only the variable behavior into subclasses. A common error is making prepareBeverage non-final; that allows subclasses to change step order, defeating the pattern. Another mistake is duplicating common steps across subclasses; instead, put shared behaviors in the base class. When testing, construct each concrete maker and call prepareBeverage; the output will show the predictable order with varying details. This pattern is especially useful for multi-step processes that must stay consistent, like build pipelines or report generation, because it guarantees the sequence while making the steps extensible. BeverageMaker Example — Template Method in Java means template method preparebeverage is final; subclasses implement varying brew and addcondiments steps so behavior differs while order remains constant.. In practical terms, preparebeverage final method and subclass overrides. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: BeverageMaker pattern
keyIdea.text: Template method prepareBeverage is final; subclasses implement varying brew and addCondiments steps so behavior differs while order remains constant.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › BeverageMaker Demo
Abstract class
abstract class BeverageMaker {
  public final void prepareBeverage(){
    boilWater(); brew(); pourInCup(); addCondiments();
  }
  private void boilWater(){ System.out.println("Boiling water"); }
  protected abstract void brew();
  private void pourInCup(){ System.out.println("Pouring into cup"); }
  protected abstract void addCondiments();
}
Concrete classes
class CoffeeMaker extends BeverageMaker{
  protected void brew(){ System.out.println("Dripping coffee through filter"); }
  protected void addCondiments(){ System.out.println("Adding sugar and milk"); }
}
class TeaMaker extends BeverageMaker{
  protected void brew(){ System.out.println("Steeping the tea bag"); }
  protected void addCondiments(){ System.out.println("Adding lemon"); }
}
Running prepareBeverage on each concrete maker prints the same high-level steps, with different brew and condiment messages reflecting subclass behavior.

screens.title: ReportGenerator — Apply Template Method
screens.subtitle: Design a template for report generation with concrete subclasses

narration.text: Apply Template Method to report generation. The abstract ReportGenerator defines a final generateReport method that sequences fetching raw data, processing it, formatting output, and saving the result. Subclasses implement fetchData, processData, and formatOutput to provide format-specific behavior such as H T M L or PDF. The base class can supply a concrete saveReport helper to avoid duplication. When implementing HtmlReportGenerator, fetchData might simulate a database call, processData prepares the H T M L body, and formatOutput wraps content in H T M L tags. For PdfReportGenerator, fetchData may simulate an external A P I, processData aggregates content differently, and formatOutput returns a simulated PDF string. Designing the template this way enforces consistent steps for all report types and makes it easy to add new formats by creating new subclasses. Be mindful to keep generateReport final so subclasses cannot change the order. Test each generator by calling generateReport and inspecting the formatted output; verify saveReport receives the produced content and that the first 50 characters are logged. This activity reinforces how Template Method ensures process consistency while allowing flexible representations of output.

keyIdea.title: ReportGenerator template
keyIdea.text: Use a final generateReport method that calls abstract fetchData, processData, and formatOutput to produce different report types safely.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › ReportGenerator Activity
Template skeleton
abstract class ReportGenerator{
  public final void generateReport(){
    System.out.println("--- Starting Report Generation ---");
    Object raw = fetchData();
    Object processed = processData(raw);
    String out = formatOutput(processed);
    saveReport(out);
    System.out.println("--- Report Generation Finished ---");
  }
  protected abstract Object fetchData();
  protected abstract Object processData(Object rawData);
  protected abstract String formatOutput(Object processedData);
  protected void saveReport(String content){ System.out.println("Saving report content (first 50 chars): " + content.substring(0, Math.min(content.length(),50)) + "..."); }
}
Concrete generators
class HtmlReportGenerator extends ReportGenerator{ /* implements fetchData, processData, formatOutput */ }
class PdfReportGenerator extends ReportGenerator{ /* implements fetchData, processData, formatOutput */ }
Run generateReport on each concrete class to see consistent sequencing with different formatted outputs. This demonstrates the Template Method in a practical scenario.

screens.title: Iterator vs Template Method
screens.subtitle: When to use each pattern and how they complement each other

narration.text: Both patterns address different concerns and can be used together. Use Iterator when your primary need is to provide uniform, encapsulated traversal over elements in a collection. Use Template Method when you have a fixed multi-step process where steps vary by implementation. They complement each other when a template method needs to process elements obtained from a collection: the template can fetch data using an iterator so the processing step is abstracted from the collection details. Consider trade-offs: Iterator adds small object creation overhead for each iterator instance but improves modularity and testability. Template Method centralizes algorithm structure but requires careful A P I design so subclasses do not break the order. A common design mistake is confusing the two: don’t use Template Method to implement traversal mechanics — that responsibility belongs to an iterator. Conversely, don’t force traversal-specific concerns into a template class. When both patterns are justified, prefer small, focused classes: an iterator for traversal, a template class for algorithm orchestration, and concrete subclasses or iterators to vary behavior. Finally, follow the Open/Closed Principle: add new iterators or subclasses rather than modifying existing code.

keyIdea.title: Pattern selection
keyIdea.text: Iterator handles traversal; Template Method handles algorithm structure. Use both when a template needs to process elements from varied collections.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Pattern Comparison
Iterator
  • Goal: uniform traversal without exposing internals
  • Key parts: Iterator + ConcreteIterator + Aggregate
  • Use when collections vary in representation
Template Method
  • Goal: fix algorithm order while varying steps
  • Key parts: Abstract class with template method and hooks
  • Use when a high-level process is constant across variants
Combined usage

When a template method needs to operate on a collection, have it obtain an iterator from the aggregate, then call abstract processing steps for each element. This keeps traversal and processing concerns separated and extensible.

screens.title: Implementation Tips, Pitfalls, and Testing
screens.subtitle: Design choices, fail-fast behavior, and unit testing strategies

narration.text: When you implement these patterns, follow a few practical best practices and test strategies. For iterators, keep state private, document whether the iterator is fail-fast or weakly consistent, and consider capturing a modification count in the iterator constructor to detect structural changes. For Template Method, make the template method final to prevent subclasses from altering the algorithm order. Provide sensible default implementations for hooks so subclasses only override what they need. In tests, validate edge cases: an empty collection should result in hasNext returning false and next throwing NoSuchElementException; calling prepareBeverage on different concrete classes should produce outputs in the exact expected sequence. Write unit tests for both happy paths and failure modes: concurrent modification detection for iterators and missing hook behavior for template classes. When you need concurrency, evaluate concurrent collection types instead of rolling your own synchronization within iterators. Finally, favor small classes with single responsibilities: an iterator for traversal, an aggregate for storage and iterator creation, and subclasses that implement algorithm steps. These choices make the code easier to reason about, change, and extend safely. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Testing & safety
keyIdea.text: Test empty and end-of-iteration cases; make template methods final and choose fail-fast or concurrent-safe iterators appropriately.

Iterator tips
  • Keep internal state private
  • Decide fail-fast vs. concurrent-safe
  • Avoid exposing backing storage
Template tips

  • Provide concrete shared steps in base class
  • Use hooks for optional behavior

narration.text: Quickly review the essential concepts from this chapter. The Iterator pattern provides a standard traversal interface — hasNext and next — that hides the collection's internal representation and reduces coupling. An aggregate creates iterators, and concrete iterators encapsulate traversal state. The Template Method pattern defines an algorithm's skeleton in a base class while delegating variable steps to subclasses via abstract methods and optional hooks. Always mark the template method final to protect the algorithm's order. Common practical notes: do not modify collections while iterating without synchronization or a concurrent-safe design, and prefer small, single-purpose classes for iterators and template implementations. When both patterns are needed, the template can obtain an iterator to process collection elements, keeping traversal and processing concerns separated. These practices improve maintainability, promote the Open/Closed Principle, and make your code easier to extend safely.

keyIdea.title: Concise takeaway
keyIdea.text: Iterator = safe traversal; Template Method = fixed sequence with customizable steps. Use both to keep code modular and extensible.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Key Concepts
Iterator Pattern
Provides hasNext and next so clients iterate without knowledge of the backing structure.
Template Method
Defines algorithm skeleton in base class; subclasses override abstract steps to vary behavior.
Best Practices
Keep iterators minimal, mark template methods final, and test edge cases like empty collections and concurrent modifications.
Final summary

Use iterator for traversal concerns and template method for algorithm orchestration. Combine them when a template must process collection elements, keeping responsibilities separate.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact cards to recall the essentials

narration.text: Keep three quick reminders with you as you code. First, iterators are the centralized way to traverse collections: implement hasNext and next and avoid exposing internals. Second, template methods fix algorithm order: make the template final and move variable steps into abstract methods and hooks. Third, test edge cases and concurrency concerns: empty collections, end-of-iteration exceptions, and concurrent modifications must be covered by tests or by choosing appropriate concurrent-safe structures. These three items will steer your design decisions and help you write modular, extensible code. Iterator
hasNext and next separate traversal concerns from storage details.
Template Method
A final template keeps step order; subclasses implement the variable steps.
Testing
Cover empty cases, end-of-iteration exceptions, and concurrent modification behaviors in tests.
Bottom line

Choose the pattern that matches the problem: iterator for traversal, template for algorithm structure, and combine them when processing collections inside a fixed process.
